notes.front: What problem does Kubernetes solve?
notes.back: It's a container orchestrator: it abstracts the underlying infrastructure and automatically schedules, runs, monitors, scales, and reschedules containerized apps across a cluster of nodes, so you declare desired state rather than managing individual machines.

notes.front: What are the two node roles in a Kubernetes cluster?
notes.back:
• Master / control plane node(s) — run the components that control and manage the cluster.
  • Worker nodes — run your actual containerized applications.

notes.front: Name the four control plane components.
notes.back:
• API server — front end you and other components talk to.
  • Scheduler — assigns pods to nodes.
  • Controller Manager — runs the controllers (reconciliation loops).
  • etcd — distributed key-value store holding all cluster state.

notes.front: Name the three components running on every worker node.
notes.back:
• Kubelet — talks to the API server and manages containers on its node.
  • Kube-proxy — load-balances network traffic to Service backends.
  • Container runtime — (containerd, CRI-O, etc.) actually runs the containers.

notes.front: What is kubectl?
notes.back: The command-line client that sends requests to the API server to create, read, update, and delete cluster resources.

notes.front: What is a Pod?
notes.back: The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes: a group of one or more containers that share the same network namespace (one IP, shared ports) and can share storage volumes. Containers in a pod are always co-located and co-scheduled on the same node.

notes.front: Why would you put multiple containers in one Pod instead of one each?
notes.back: Only when they're tightly coupled and must run together — e.g. a main app plus a sidecar (log shipper, proxy, adapter) that needs to share the same network/filesystem. Independent components should go in separate pods so they can scale independently.

notes.front: What are labels and how are they used?
notes.back: Arbitrary key-value pairs attached to resources for organization. Label selectors then let you filter and operate on subsets of resources (e.g. a Service selecting all pods with app=web). Labels are the primary grouping mechanism in Kubernetes.

notes.front: What are namespaces for?
notes.back: They partition resources into isolated groups (scoping, multi-tenancy, name uniqueness within the namespace). Note: namespaces don't provide network isolation by themselves — that requires NetworkPolicies.

notes.front: What is a liveness probe and what are its three mechanisms?
notes.back:
A periodic check the kubelet runs to decide whether to restart a container. Mechanisms:
  • HTTP GET — 2xx/3xx = healthy.
  • TCP socket — connection opens = healthy.
  • Exec — command exit code 0 = healthy.

notes.front: What does a ReplicationController do?
notes.back: Keeps a specified number of pod replicas running, recreating them if they die or are deleted. (Legacy — superseded by ReplicaSet, which is itself usually managed by a Deployment.)

notes.front: How does a ReplicaSet differ from a ReplicationController?
notes.back: A ReplicaSet is the newer generation with more expressive set-based label selectors (e.g. in, notin, exists), whereas a ReplicationController only supports equality-based selectors. You rarely create ReplicaSets directly — Deployments manage them.

notes.front: What is a DaemonSet?
notes.back: A controller that runs exactly one copy of a pod on every node (or every node matching a selector). Used for node-level agents: log collectors, monitoring agents, kube-proxy, CNI plugins.

notes.front: Difference between a Job and a CronJob?
notes.back:
• Job — runs one or more pods to completion for a finite task, then stops (not restarted on success).
  • CronJob — creates Jobs on a repeating schedule using cron syntax.

notes.front: What is a Service and why is it needed?
notes.back: A stable network endpoint (single virtual IP + DNS name) that load-balances across a dynamic set of pods selected by labels. Needed because pod IPs are ephemeral — pods come and go — so clients need a fixed address to reach them.

notes.front: What does a ClusterIP Service provide?
notes.back: A virtual IP reachable only from inside the cluster. This is the default Service type, used for internal service-to-service communication.

notes.front: What does a NodePort Service do?
notes.back: Exposes the Service on a static port (default range 30000–32767) on every node's IP, so external traffic hitting <nodeIP>:<nodePort> is routed to the Service. Builds on ClusterIP.

notes.front: What does a LoadBalancer Service do?
notes.back: Provisions an external load balancer from the cloud provider that fronts the Service and forwards to the NodePort/ClusterIP. Gives the Service a single externally reachable IP. Builds on NodePort.

notes.front: What is an Endpoints object?
notes.back: The list of actual pod IP:port pairs currently backing a Service. The Service selects pods by label; the Endpoints (or EndpointSlices) controller keeps this list in sync as pods come and go.

notes.front: What is an Ingress and why use it over many LoadBalancer Services?
notes.back: An Ingress is an HTTP(S) routing layer (host/path-based) that exposes many Services through a single external entry point managed by an Ingress controller. Cheaper and more flexible than one cloud load balancer per Service.

notes.front: What is a headless Service?
notes.back: A Service with clusterIP: None. Instead of a single virtual IP, DNS returns the individual pod IPs directly. Used when clients need to address specific pods — e.g. StatefulSets.

notes.front: What is a readiness probe and how does it differ from a liveness probe?
notes.back: A readiness probe decides whether a pod should receive traffic — failing it removes the pod from Service endpoints (no restart). A liveness probe decides whether to restart the container. Readiness gates traffic; liveness gates lifecycle.

notes.front: What is an emptyDir volume?
notes.back: A volume created empty when the pod is scheduled and deleted when the pod is removed. Lives as long as the pod; useful for scratch space or sharing files between containers in the same pod.

notes.front: What is a hostPath volume and its main caveat?
notes.back: Mounts a file or directory from the node's own filesystem into the pod. Caveat: data is tied to a specific node, so it's not portable if the pod is rescheduled elsewhere — generally only for node-level system pods.

notes.front: Persistent Volume (PV) vs Persistent Volume Claim (PVC)?
notes.back:
• PV — a piece of storage in the cluster, provisioned by an admin or dynamically. Cluster-level resource.
  • PVC — a user's request for storage (size, access mode) that binds to a matching PV.
This decouples app authors from storage details.

notes.front: What does a StorageClass enable?
notes.back: Dynamic provisioning: when a PVC references a StorageClass, a matching PersistentVolume is created on demand by the associated provisioner — no pre-provisioned PVs required.

notes.front: What are the PV access modes?
notes.back:
• ReadWriteOnce (RWO) — mounted read-write by a single node.
  • ReadOnlyMany (ROX) — read-only by many nodes.
  • ReadWriteMany (RWX) — read-write by many nodes.
  • ReadWriteOncePod — read-write by a single pod.

notes.front: What is a ConfigMap?
notes.back: An API object holding non-sensitive configuration as key-value pairs, decoupled from the image. Consumed by pods as environment variables, command-line args, or files in a mounted volume.

notes.front: How is a Secret different from a ConfigMap?
notes.back: Functionally similar (key-value config injected as env vars or files), but intended for sensitive data. Values are base64-encoded in the object and can be kept out of node disk (tmpfs). Note: base64 is encoding, not encryption — enable encryption-at-rest in etcd and RBAC for real protection.

notes.front: What happens when you mount a ConfigMap as a volume and then update it?
notes.back: The mounted files are eventually updated automatically (kubelet sync, with some delay). However, values injected as environment variables are NOT updated — the pod must be restarted to pick those up.

notes.front: What is the Downward API?
notes.back: A mechanism to expose a pod's own metadata (name, namespace, labels, annotations, resource requests/limits, node name, pod IP) to its containers via environment variables or files, without calling the API server.

notes.front: What does a Deployment add over a bare ReplicaSet?
notes.back: Declarative updates with controlled rollout strategies and easy rollback. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets under the hood, creating a new one for each revision and shifting pods between them.

notes.front: Compare the RollingUpdate and Recreate deployment strategies.
notes.back:
• RollingUpdate (default) — gradually replaces old pods with new ones; no downtime.
  • Recreate — kills all old pods first, then creates new ones; causes downtime but guarantees no two versions run at once.

notes.front: What do maxSurge and maxUnavailable control?
notes.back:
RollingUpdate pacing:
  • maxSurge — how many pods above the desired count may exist during the update.
  • maxUnavailable — how many pods may be unavailable during the update.

notes.front: How do you roll back a Deployment?
notes.back: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> (optionally --to-revision=N). Kubernetes keeps old ReplicaSets (up to revisionHistoryLimit) so it can scale a previous one back up.

notes.front: What does a StatefulSet provide that a Deployment doesn't?
notes.back: Stable, sticky per-pod identity: predictable ordinal names (web-0, web-1…), stable network IDs via a headless Service, and stable per-pod persistent storage that survives rescheduling. Pods are created/deleted in order.

notes.front: Why does a StatefulSet require a headless Service?
notes.back: To give each pod a stable DNS name (<pod>.<service>.<ns>.svc) so peers can address specific instances directly — essential for clustered stateful systems (databases, message brokers).

notes.front: How does per-pod storage work in a StatefulSet?
notes.back: Via volumeClaimTemplates: each pod gets its own PVC (and thus PV). When a pod is rescheduled, it reattaches to the same PVC, preserving its data and identity.

notes.front: What is etcd's role?
notes.back: A distributed, consistent key-value store (uses the Raft consensus algorithm) that is the single source of truth for all cluster state. Only the API server talks to it directly.

notes.front: What is the API server's role in the architecture?
notes.back: The central hub: it validates and persists resource objects to etcd and is the only component that reads/writes etcd. All other components watch it for changes and never talk to each other directly.

notes.front: What does the Scheduler actually do?
notes.back: Watches for newly created pods with no assigned node, then selects a suitable node (filtering by constraints, then scoring/prioritizing) and writes the node assignment back. It doesn't run the pod — the kubelet does.

notes.front: What is the Controller Manager?
notes.back: A process running many controllers, each a reconciliation loop watching the API server and driving actual state toward desired state (ReplicaSet controller, Deployment controller, Node controller, Endpoints controller, etc.).

notes.front: What is the kubelet's job?
notes.back: The node agent: watches the API server for pods assigned to its node, instructs the container runtime to run them, monitors their health (probes), and reports status back to the API server.

notes.front: What does kube-proxy do?
notes.back: Implements Services on each node by programming the data plane (iptables or IPVS mode) so traffic to a Service's virtual IP is load-balanced across the backing pod endpoints.

notes.front: Explain the watch mechanism and reconciliation loop.
notes.back: Components don't poll; they watch the API server for changes to resources they care about. Each controller continuously compares desired state (spec) to observed state (status) and takes corrective action — the core 'control loop' / declarative model of Kubernetes.

notes.front: What networking guarantee must a Kubernetes pod network satisfy?
notes.back: Every pod gets its own IP and all pods can reach all other pods directly without NAT, regardless of node. This flat network is implemented by a CNI (Container Network Interface) plugin.

notes.front: What is the pause / infrastructure container?
notes.back: A tiny container that holds the pod's shared network (and IPC) namespace. App containers join its namespace, so they share one IP even as individual app containers restart.

notes.front: What is a ServiceAccount?
notes.back: An identity for processes running in pods (as opposed to human users). Each pod runs as a ServiceAccount, whose token can be mounted so the app can authenticate to the API server.

notes.front: What does Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) consist of?
notes.back:
• Role / ClusterRole — a set of allowed verbs on resources (namespaced vs cluster-wide).
  • RoleBinding / ClusterRoleBinding — grants a Role/ClusterRole to a user, group, or ServiceAccount.

notes.front: Role vs ClusterRole?
notes.back: A Role grants permissions within a single namespace. A ClusterRole grants permissions cluster-wide or to cluster-scoped resources (nodes, PVs) and can be reused across namespaces via RoleBindings.

notes.front: What are the three stages a request passes through at the API server?
notes.back:
• Authentication — who are you? (certs, tokens, ServiceAccounts).
  • Authorization — are you allowed? (RBAC).
  • Admission control — mutate/validate the request (e.g. defaulting, policy webhooks).

notes.front: What is a SecurityContext?
notes.back: Pod- or container-level settings controlling security: runAsUser/runAsNonRoot, privileged mode, capabilities to add/drop, read-only root filesystem, SELinux options, etc.

notes.front: What does a NetworkPolicy do?
notes.back: Defines allowed ingress/egress traffic for pods selected by labels — effectively a firewall between pods. Without any policy, all pod-to-pod traffic is allowed; a policy enforcement requires a CNI plugin that supports it.

notes.front: What was PodSecurityPolicy and what replaced it?
notes.back: A (now-removed) cluster-level resource controlling security-sensitive pod fields. Replaced by Pod Security Admission (built-in admission controller enforcing the Pod Security Standards: privileged / baseline / restricted).

notes.front: Requests vs limits for CPU and memory?
notes.back:
• Request — the guaranteed amount; used by the scheduler to place the pod and reserved on the node.
  • Limit — the hard cap. Exceeding a CPU limit throttles; exceeding a memory limit gets the container OOM-killed.

notes.front: Name the three Quality of Service (QoS) classes and how they're determined.
notes.back:
• Guaranteed — every container has requests == limits for both CPU and memory.
  • Burstable — at least one request set, but not Guaranteed.
  • BestEffort — no requests or limits set.
Under node memory pressure, BestEffort pods are evicted first, then Burstable, then Guaranteed.

notes.front: LimitRange vs ResourceQuota?
notes.back:
• LimitRange — per-object defaults/min/max for requests and limits within a namespace.
  • ResourceQuota — aggregate caps on total resource consumption (and object counts) across a whole namespace.

notes.front: What does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) do?
notes.back: Automatically adjusts the replica count of a workload based on observed metrics (CPU/memory utilization or custom metrics) to keep them near a target. It scales pods out/in, not resources within a pod.

notes.front: HPA vs Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) vs Cluster Autoscaler?
notes.back:
• HPA — changes the number of pod replicas.
  • VPA — adjusts a pod's CPU/memory requests/limits.
  • Cluster Autoscaler — adds/removes nodes when pods can't be scheduled or nodes are underused.

notes.front: What is the difference between nodeSelector and node affinity?
notes.back: Both steer pods to nodes by labels. nodeSelector is a simple hard equality match. Node affinity is more expressive — supports operators and both required (hard) and preferred (soft) rules.

notes.front: How do taints and tolerations work together?
notes.back: A taint on a node repels pods that don't tolerate it (effects: NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, NoExecute). A pod with a matching toleration is allowed onto the tainted node. Taints push away; tolerations grant exceptions.

notes.front: Node affinity vs pod affinity/anti-affinity?
notes.back:
• Node affinity — attracts pods to nodes based on node labels.
  • Pod affinity — co-locates a pod near other pods matching a selector (same topology domain).
  • Pod anti-affinity — keeps pods apart (e.g. spread replicas across nodes/zones).

notes.front: What is a Custom Resource Definition (CRD)?
notes.back: A way to register your own resource type with the API server, so you can create and manage custom objects (e.g. kind: Database) using the standard kubectl/API tooling, stored in etcd like built-in resources.

notes.front: What is the Operator pattern?
notes.back: A custom controller paired with one or more CRDs that encodes operational/domain knowledge for an application. It watches custom resources and reconciles real-world state (provisioning, backups, upgrades) — automating what a human operator would do.
